title: Clothes moth treatment
subtitle: Based on official Australian sources, Mitch's past jobs and the product labels, checked against NSW requirements. Mitch will show you his own method on the ride-along. Updated 6 Nov 2026.
source: LPC Tech Onboarding Pack (PPE, never list, if something goes wrong); jobbook-data/chemicals.json (Clothes Moth Treatment products); jobbook-data/services.json (past wordings); what it looks like, where to look and customer advice from Australian Museum, Museums Victoria, WA Museum, Queensland Museum and Better Health Channel (not from Mitch); what it looks like, where to look and customer advice from Australian Museum, Museums Victoria, WA Museum, Queensland Museum and Better Health Channel (not from Mitch)

sections.heading: When this job comes up
body: Customer has clothes moths or carpet moths, or silverfish. Mitch's service is called Clothes Moth Treatment, and silverfish jobs have been written up as Specialist Treatment. Past invoices read: "Moth & Silverfish treatment", "Moth & Silverfish second treatment", "Carpet moth treatment" and "Rug moth treatment, 6 rugs (both sides treated)".

Two clothes moths are common here and both were brought in from overseas: the case-bearing clothes moth and the webbing clothes moth. The adult moths are not what damages things. The grubs are. They go for animal fibres like wool, silk, fur and feathers.
The job process, the never list, PPE and the free service period are in the Every job guide.

sections.heading: What the law and the label require

items.text: Follow the product label
items.detail: Using a pesticide against its label is an offence. If the job needs something the label does not allow, stop and call Mitch.

items.text: Make the record the same day
items.detail: Every pesticide job needs a record: full product name, date, target pest, rate and quantity, address and area treated, who applied it, equipment, and start and finish times. It must be made within 48 hours and kept at least 3 years. Give the customer a copy if they ask.

items.text: Only do work your licence covers
items.detail: If a treatment is outside your licence class, work under Mitch's direct supervision and do not do it alone.

items.text: Protect people, pets and the environment
items.detail: Wear the PPE the label and SDS call for. Keep spray and bait away from people, pets, food, drains and waterways. Harming people, wildlife or property with a pesticide is an offence.

items.text: Roof voids and subfloors: asbestos
items.detail: Houses built before 1990 can have asbestos (roof insulation, eaves, cladding). Do not disturb anything that might be asbestos. Stop and tell Mitch.

items.text: Roof voids: live wiring
items.detail: Look first. Do not touch cables. If you are not sure it is safe, do not go in and tell Mitch.

items.text: Tight or stuffy spaces
items.detail: If you cannot get out easily, or the air feels wrong, do not go in. Tell Mitch first.

sections.heading: How to tell what you have
rows: Grub living in a little silk case it drags around
Case-bearing clothes moth. Cases and droppings (frass) are the signs, for example a case inside a felt hat.
Creamy-white grub with a dark head, under silky webbing or tunnels
Webbing clothes moth. Fully grown it is about 12 mm.
Small woven cases stuck to a bare wall or ceiling
Can mean pupae (the stage before the moth).
Small moth in the wardrobe or drawers
Adults avoid light and hide in dark places like wardrobes and drawers. The case-bearing moth is about 1 cm.
Small, brown, hairy grub, no case or webbing
Carpet beetle. See the Carpet beetle guide.
Wingless, shiny, scaly, with three tails
Silverfish, not a moth. Up to about 2 cm, long antennae. Eats paper, glue, cotton and other fibres.

items.text: Wardrobes and drawers
items.detail: Adult moths hide in dark places like these.

items.text: Carpet edges, along skirting boards, under furniture and inside cupboards
items.detail: Grubs feed in undisturbed spots like these.

items.text: Dusty, dirty or stained wool, silk, fur, feather and felt items
items.detail: Moths lay eggs on dirty cloth and go for fabric with sweat or spilled drinks on it.

items.text: Dark, quiet, humid, out-of-the-way spots near paper, books and cotton (silverfish)
Roof void
items.detail: Mitch will show you how on the ride-along. Until then, follow the product label.

sections.title: PPE on before you go in
sections.note: Never apply chemicals without PPE. If the SDS requires it, you wear it. No exceptions.
items: Gloves and closed shoes at minimum
Gloves, mask and eye protection for any spray, as per the product SDS

sections.heading: Steps
sections.title: Steps
sections.note: Where to look and the safety steps are from official sources and are marked. How Mitch treats it is still to confirm.
items: Ask the customer to point out where they have seen the moths or the damage

items.text: Check for the signs
items.detail: Little silk cases, webbing, droppings (frass) and eaten patches in wool, silk and fur.

items: Take BEFORE photos of the problem areas

items.text: Move pets, birdcages and fish tanks out of the way. Cover or remove food and personal items in the area you are treating
items.detail: Many pesticides are highly toxic to birds and fish.

items.text: Treat rugs on both sides
items.detail: A past invoice reads "6 rugs (both sides treated)". Mitch treats both sides of a rug. Ask him how.

items.text: Treat the other areas Mitch has told you to
items.detail: Mitch will show you how on the ride-along. Until then, follow the product label.

items.text: Keep surface sprays to out-of-the-way spots like along skirting boards, not on furniture or things people touch
Apply per the product label. Never exceed label rates
items.detail: Never mix chemicals without checking the label first. If in doubt, call Mitch.

items: Keep chemicals away from food, children and pets
Note anything you could not treat or reach, and why

sections.heading: Job complete when
items: Areas treated as agreed with Mitch
Anything you could not treat or reach is noted on the job report, with the reason
Product, rate, area and quantity recorded on the job report
Customer told what you did and what to expect (see "If the customer asks" below)

items.text: Customer told to keep wardrobes, drawers and storage clean, tidy and dust-free, and to vacuum carpet edges, skirting boards, under furniture and inside wardrobes

items: Customer given the re-entry time: follow the product label. The Every job guide says 1 to 2 hours once dry
Service report left, or customer told it is being emailed

items.a: Clothes moths. Two kinds are common here. It's the little grubs that eat the cloth, not the moths. They like wool, silk, fur and feathers.
Moths lay their eggs on dirty cloth, and they're drawn to fabric with sweat or spilled drinks on it. They hide in dark, undisturbed spots like wardrobes, drawers and the back of cupboards.

items.q: What can I do to help?
items.a: Keep wardrobes, drawers and storage areas clean, tidy and dust-free. Vacuum the edges of carpet, along skirting boards, under furniture and inside wardrobes. Check now and then for the first signs.

items.q: Is it safe for the kids and pets?
items.a: Keep kids and pets out of the area while we treat. Follow the product label for when it's safe to come back in. We normally say 1 to 2 hours once it's dry.

items.q: Can you save my damaged wool or silk, or my good rug?
items.a: Our job is the moths. If it's a precious or badly damaged piece, a textile conservator is the one to ask before anything is done to it.

items.q: Is a silverfish the same thing?
items.a: No. Silverfish are a different bug. They're wingless and shiny with three tails, and they eat paper, glue and cotton.

sections.heading: Tell Mitch straight away if
sections.body: Call Mitch on 0432 181 689. After hours or urgent, call Mitch directly.

items.text: You apply the wrong chemical
items.detail: Stop immediately. Do not continue. Call Mitch.

items.text: There is a spill
items.detail: Follow the SDS procedure. Call Mitch immediately. Never leave a spill unattended.

items.text: Someone is hurt
items.detail: Treat the injury first. Call Mitch. Write down what happened.

items.text: The customer complains or gets aggressive
items.detail: Stay calm and do not argue. For a complaint, tell them Mitch will call them today. If they are aggressive, remove yourself. Call Mitch either way.

items.text: The customer asks for a quote on anything complex, or you are not sure
items.detail: Say "I'll need to get Mitch to come and have a look and provide a quote for that."

items.text: You see signs of termites or other pests outside this job
items.detail: Photograph it and tell Mitch. Termite quotes always go to Mitch.
